name: The Mochi Tree of Hogon-ji

location.address: Hogon-ji Temple, Chikubushima Island, 1664 Hayazaki-cho, Nagahama, Shiga Prefecture (滋賀県長浜市早崎町1664), beside the three-story pagoda

access: Paid entry: Chikubushima is a small uninhabited island in Lake Biwa reached only by scheduled ferry from Nagahama, Hikone or Imazu; the temple grounds themselves also charge an entry fee. Not walkable from any city centre and needs a boat crossing and a schedule, honestly stated rather than described as a walk.
transport: Ferry from Nagahama, Hikone or Imazu port (roughly 30-40 min crossing depending on port); the temple is a short climb of stone steps from the island jetty.
verify_notes: Planted in 1602 (Keicho 7) by Katagiri Katsumoto, the Toyotomi-era construction supervisor, as a commemorative planting when he relocated the Kannon Hall, the Chinese Gate (Karamon, now a National Treasure moved from Hideyoshi's Osaka Castle) and the covered corridor bridge to Hogon-ji -- documented planting date for this specific specimen, from the temple's own website, not a bridge from the site's general history. Species: the common name "mochi" (moch-no-ki) is the standard Japanese name for Ilex integra, and Commons categorises this specimen's photos accordingly; no source gives a scientific name explicitly so treat the species as reasonably well established by naming convention rather than independently confirmed. No girth or height published anywhere I found. Stands beside the temple's three-story pagoda; I could not find a tree-level coordinate, only the temple/island address, so the pin is approximate at temple level on a small island. Newest photographic evidence of the tree is Commons photos dated December 2016; no more recent sighting found, so "alive now" rests on a 10-year-old photo plus the temple being an actively maintained, frequently visited National Treasure site with no news of loss. A second, different tree also grows at Hogon-ji (a Gleditsia japonica / Japanese honey locust) documented separately on Commons; do not conflate the two when writing the story.
